item.research_question: Does a single-phase high entropy alloy exhibit inverse Hall-Petch behavior and low friction/wear in an ultra-high vacuum environment, and what is the underlying mechanism?
item.material_system: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (FCC single-phase)
item.processing_route: Laser Engineered Net Shaping (LENS) additive manufacturing using 45–75 µm gas atomized powder; laser power 350–400 W, build velocity 400–600 mm/min, layer thickness 250–300 µm, hatch spacing 800 µm, in <50 ppm O2 atmosphere; initial average grain size ~42 µm
item.test_conditions: Ultra-high vacuum (~10⁻⁹ torr), room temperature, rotary sliding with 3.2 mm sapphire sphere, loads of 10 mN and 100 mN, angular velocity ~15.5 rpm, stroke length 45°, up to 20k cycles
key_findings: Steady-state friction coefficients of μss ≅ 0.32 at 10 mN and μss ≅ 0.68 at 100 mN were measured in UHV.
Specific wear rates were remarkably low at ~10⁻⁶ mm³/N-m for the initially soft, coarse-grained material.
STEM validation showed dynamic grain refinement to an average size of d = 13 ± 5 nm (upper bound) or 2–3 nm during sliding, with amorphous regions present.
A pause in sliding for 24 hours caused the friction coefficient to increase to μ ≅ 0.55, implying grain growth to ~5 nm.
The dynamic amorphization model predicted an average high angle grain boundary energy of 0.87 J/m².
Cavitation-induced nanoporosity was observed in the highly deformed surface layer, linked to the predicted high grain boundary energy.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute low friction and wear to shear-induced dynamic amorphization and extreme grain refinement below a critical size (dcrit ≅ 10–50 nm), where grain boundary sliding becomes energetically favorable over dislocation activity, leading to inverse Hall-Petch behavior and a near-amorphous surface layer.
item.limitations: Ex situ techniques like TEM and nanoindentation are not ideal for determining the actual grain size during sliding because the ultra-nanocrystalline surface layers are extremely thin and prone to rapid grain growth and recrystallization after the test.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that the observed phenomena may indicate low temperature and high strain rate superplasticity, implying a need to further explore the link between grain boundary decohesion, cavitation, and superplasticity in HEAs.
quotes: Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m)
This model of grain size-dependent shear strength requires no fitting parameters and is based exclusively on materials properties
The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer
